title: Gateau Saint-Honore
subtitle: classic French celebration cake with choux, caramel, and chiboust cream
excerpt: Gateau Saint-Honore is a French celebration cake built on a puff pastry disc, ringed with a choux border, topped with caramel-dipped profiteroles, and filled with chiboust cream. You get multiple textures in one piece: crisp pastry, soft choux, brittle caramel shell, and a cream that is simultaneously rich and airy. Watch the caramel: it is extremely hot, injures quickly, and the window between working temperature and too cool to dip is only a few minutes.
sourceNotes: Gateau Saint-Honore is named for the patron saint of pastry chefs and bakers, Saint Honore (Honoratus of Amiens). The cake was codified in French patisserie by Chiboust in the 1840s and appears in Escoffier (Le Guide Culinaire, 1903, public domain). Chiboust cream (pastry cream lightened with Italian meringue) is named after the original pastry chef.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the puff pastry base and choux puffs up to 6 hours ahead and keep uncovered at room temperature. Make the pastry cream up to 24 hours ahead. Make the Italian meringue, complete the chiboust cream, and make the caramel on the day of assembly.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius, for both the puff pastry base and the choux. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cooked paste made by beating flour into boiling butter and water, then incorporating eggs. The steam generated inside the paste during baking puffs it into a hollow shell. For Saint-Honore the choux is piped both as a ring on top of the pastry base and as small individual puffs (profiteroles) that are separately baked and then caramel-dipped.

Pastry cream (creme patissiere) lightened with Italian meringue and set with gelatine. The result is a cream that holds its shape without being as dense as pastry cream alone. It was created by pastry chef Chiboust in the 1840s specifically for the gateau that bears his cream's name. The gelatine is essential: without it the cream collapses when the Italian meringue loses its structure.

Sugar cooked to approximately 175 degrees Celsius, at which point it develops complex bitter-sweet flavour compounds. In Saint-Honore the caramel is used to dip the profiteroles, coating them in a hard, brittle glassy shell. The caramel must be worked quickly: it sets solid within minutes of leaving the heat, and reheating it risks burning.

Small choux pastry balls, baked until hollow and crisp. In Saint-Honore they are filled with chiboust cream, dipped in caramel, and arranged around the top of the cake. The caramel both glazes the profiteroles and anchors them to the choux ring.

You get a showpiece cake that combines crisp puff pastry, airy choux shells, brittle caramel, and a cream that is simultaneously rich from the pastry cream base and light from the meringue.

Watch the caramel: it reaches 175 degrees Celsius and can cause serious burns on contact with skin; have cold water at the ready and work with a long-handled spoon, keeping your face clear of any steam.

Puff pastry base
Choux pastry

items.prepNote: leaves (sheet gelatine), soaked in cold water

content.text: Method
Preparing the puff pastry base

Heat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius (conventional). Unroll the puff pastry sheet and cut a circle approximately 22 cm in diameter using a plate as a guide. Place on a lined baking tray. Dock the base all over with a fork to prevent it puffing unevenly.

Bake for 18 to 20 minutes until deep golden and crisp throughout. Transfer to a cooling rack. The base must be fully baked and crisp before assembly; a soft centre will become soggy once the cream is added.
Making and piping the choux

Make the choux paste: bring the water, butter, and salt to a full boil in a medium saucepan. Remove from heat, tip in all the flour at once, and beat vigorously until the paste pulls from the sides and forms a smooth ball. Return to low heat for 2 minutes, stirring, to dry the paste slightly. Cool for 5 minutes, then beat in the eggs gradually until the paste is glossy and drops in a slow V-shape from the spoon.

Transfer the paste to a piping bag fitted with a 1 cm plain tip. On the cooled puff pastry base, pipe a ring of choux around the outer edge of the disc. Pipe approximately 12 to 14 small rounds (profiteroles), each about 3 cm in diameter, onto a second lined baking tray. Keep them evenly sized so they dip in caramel at the same rate.

Bake the puff pastry disc with its choux ring and the separate tray of profiteroles together at 200 degrees Celsius. The profiteroles will take 20 to 25 minutes; the ring on the pastry base may take slightly longer as the base retains heat. Do not open the oven before 20 minutes. The choux is done when it is a deep golden colour all over and feels completely firm when tapped. Transfer to cooling racks and cool completely.
Making the chiboust cream

Make the pastry cream base: whisk the egg yolks, 100 g of sugar, and cornflour until pale and smooth. Heat the milk until steaming. Pour a third of the hot milk onto the egg mixture, whisking constantly to temper. Return everything to the saucepan and cook over medium heat, stirring continuously, until very thick and bubbling. Cook for a full 2 minutes after the first large bubble appears to cook out the cornflour.

Squeeze the soaked gelatine leaves to remove excess water and stir them into the hot pastry cream immediately. They will dissolve in about 30 seconds. Pour into a clean bowl, press cling film onto the surface, and leave to cool to around 35 degrees Celsius (warm but not hot). Do not let it go fully cold or the gelatine will start to set.

Make the Italian meringue: put 100 g of sugar and 30 ml of water in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Bring to 121 degrees Celsius (use a sugar thermometer). While the syrup is heating, start whisking the egg whites in a stand mixer on medium speed. When the syrup reaches 121 degrees Celsius, increase the mixer to high speed and pour the hot syrup in a thin, steady stream down the side of the bowl while the whisk is running. Continue whisking until the meringue is thick, glossy, and the bowl feels just warm rather than hot to the touch. This takes about 5 minutes.

Working quickly while the pastry cream is still warm, fold the Italian meringue into the pastry cream in three additions using a large balloon whisk or silicone spatula. Be decisive: fold, do not stir, and work in large strokes to preserve as much of the meringue volume as possible. The final chiboust cream should be airy, light, and hold a soft peak. Transfer to a piping bag fitted with a large star tip and use immediately before the gelatine sets.
Making the caramel and dipping the profiteroles

Have a bowl of iced water at hand before beginning. Combine the 200 g of caster sugar and 60 ml of water in a small, heavy saucepan. Bring to the boil without stirring, then continue cooking over medium-high heat until the caramel reaches a deep amber colour and registers 175 degrees Celsius on a sugar thermometer. Remove from heat immediately. The colour will continue to deepen slightly from the residual heat of the pan.

Working quickly and very carefully, dip the top of each profiterole into the caramel, holding it by its base. Shake off any excess and place caramel-side up on a baking mat to set. The caramel sets hard within about 30 seconds of dipping. If the caramel in the pan becomes too thick to dip, set the saucepan briefly over very low heat for 30 seconds to re-loosen. Do not reheat it repeatedly: it will continue to darken.
Assembly

Place the puff pastry base with its baked choux ring on a serving board or cake board. Pipe chiboust cream into the centre of the ring, filling the space inside generously and building it up in swirls or rosettes.

To attach the profiteroles, dip the base of each one briefly into the remaining caramel and press it immediately against the top of the choux ring. The caramel acts as glue. Work around the ring until all the profiteroles are attached, spacing them evenly. Any remaining caramel can be drizzled decoratively over the whole cake.

Refrigerate for at least 1 hour before serving, to allow the chiboust cream to set and the gelatine to firm. Serve within 3 hours of assembly. The caramel-dipped profiteroles will begin to soften if the cake is held in the refrigerator for longer than 4 hours, as the moisture in the cream gradually dissolves the caramel shell.

attrs.problem: The chiboust cream collapsed and became runny after an hour
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding the gelatine to cold pastry cream. The gelatine must dissolve fully in the hot cream; if the cream has already cooled below 50 degrees Celsius when the gelatine is added, it will not dissolve evenly and will leave lumps.
attrs.fix: Make sure the pastry cream is still hot when the soaked gelatine is stirred in, and that the gelatine leaves are squeezed of excess water first. Under-gelling is almost always a dissolution failure rather than using too little gelatine.

attrs.problem: The caramel crystallised and turned grainy instead of amber
attrs.avoid: Avoid stirring the caramel once the sugar has dissolved. Use a clean saucepan and brush down the inside of the pan with a wet pastry brush before the caramel starts to colour, to prevent crystal formation on the walls.
attrs.fix: Start again. Crystallised caramel cannot be reversed. If you see crystallisation beginning (the caramel suddenly looks sandy), add a tablespoon of water and bring it back to the boil; sometimes this dissolves the crystals before they spread.

attrs.problem: The choux profiteroles are soft rather than crisp after baking
attrs.avoid: Avoid opening the oven door before 20 minutes or removing the choux while it still looks pale. Choux must be baked to a deep colour before it will stay crisp as it cools.
attrs.fix: Pierce each profiterole on the side with a skewer as soon as it comes out of the oven, then return to the switched-off oven with the door propped ajar for 10 minutes. This lets the steam inside escape and dries the interior.

attrs.problem: The caramel on the profiteroles became sticky and lost its crunch after refrigerating
attrs.avoid: Avoid holding the assembled cake for longer than 4 hours in the refrigerator. Caramel is hygroscopic and absorbs moisture from the air and the cream over time, softening its brittle shell.
attrs.fix: Assemble the Saint-Honore no more than 3 hours before serving. If the caramel has already softened, it cannot be re-crisped.

attrs.problem: The Italian meringue deflated immediately when folded into the pastry cream
attrs.avoid: Avoid folding the meringue into pastry cream that is too hot. If the cream is above 45 degrees Celsius when the meringue is added, the heat melts the meringue structure.
attrs.fix: The pastry cream should be warm (around 35 to 38 degrees Celsius) when folded with the meringue: warm enough that the gelatine remains fluid, but cool enough that it does not cook the whites. Check the temperature with a thermometer if unsure.

content.text: Caramel reaches approximately 175 degrees Celsius during cooking. If hot caramel touches skin, run cold water over it immediately for at least ten minutes. Seek medical care if needed. Keep a bowl of iced water at your work station before starting. Use a deep saucepan to reduce splashing. Keep children and pets away from the hob during this step. Work with a long-handled spoon and keep your face clear of the pan; steam from caramel can also cause burns.
